sections.h2: Where is the Sandusky County Recorder and what does the office handle?
sections.html:
The Sandusky County Recorder is in Room 143 of 100 N. Park Ave. in Fremont, Ohio 43420, and the office is open 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM Monday through Friday. The phone number is (419) 334-6226. The office is the land records office for every parcel in the county, and its first recorded deed dates to May 16, 1822.

Staff index each document so that a title examiner can follow a parcel from one owner to the next and see any debts attached to it. That index is what a title company reads before your sale closes. For copies of recorded documents, the county site directs requests to the recorder's staff email address.

Fremont is the county seat and largest city. Bellevue and Clyde are the other two cities, and the county site also lists Gibsonburg and Woodville among the local governments. A deed for a house in any of them is recorded at the same Fremont counter.

sections.h2: What are the steps to record a deed in Sandusky County?
sections.html:
A deed moves through the auditor first and the recorder second. The recorder indexes it last, so a seller who skips an earlier step loses time at the counter.

  • Have the deed drafted with the full legal description. Pull the description from the last recorded deed for the parcel, which you can find in the county's public search.
  • Sign the deed in front of a notary or another officer Ohio law lists for acknowledgments.
  • Take the deed to the Sandusky County Auditor, Room 109 at 100 N. Park Ave., telephone (419) 334-6123, with the statement of value the state requires.
  • Pay the auditor's conveyance fee and any county transfer tax that applies.
  • Present the endorsed deed to the recorder, pay the recording fee, and ask how the original will be returned.

A title company or closing attorney can file the deed for you, often electronically. If you are transferring a deed without a sale, such as a gift to a child, ask the auditor which exemption form applies before you go.

sections.h2: What does Ohio law require before a deed can be recorded?
sections.html:
The grantor must sign the deed, and the signing must be acknowledged before a judge or clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor, who certifies the acknowledgment (R.C. 5301.01). A deed that is not properly acknowledged is not ready for the recorder.

Recording itself matters for a practical reason. Under R.C. 5301.25, a deed or similar instrument for land must be recorded in the county where the property sits, and until it is recorded it is treated as fraudulent against a later buyer who bought in good faith without knowing about it. If you sell to a buyer and the deed sits unrecorded, a second claimant could gain priority.

When a survey was made of the land being conveyed, the same section requires the surveyor's name to appear in the deed, in a statement worded "A survey of this property was made by" followed by the name. Ask your closing agent whether your deed needs that line.

sections.h2: What recording fees does Ohio law set for a deed?
sections.html:
Ohio sets the base recording fees in R.C. 317.32, and each charge has a base part and a housing trust fund part. A county may add a document preservation surcharge of up to five dollars, so the recorder's counter price can be higher than the statute's base figures. Ask the Sandusky County Recorder for the posted fee list before you send a check.

Recording charges as printed in R.C. 317.32 (Ohio Revised Code, codes.ohio.gov)
ServiceBase feeHousing trust fund fee
Record and index, first two pages$17$17
Each added page, 8.5 by 14 inches or fraction$4$4
Certify a copy, per page$1$1
Photocopy after recording, per page$1$1
Marginal reference by separate instrument$2$2

The same statute allows a document preservation surcharge of up to five dollars, which goes to the county general fund. Fees are paid when the instrument is presented. Electronic recording may be paid by electronic funds transfer or another electronic means after presentation.

sections.h2: How do the conveyance fee and transfer tax work with a deed?
sections.html:
Before the auditor endorses a deed for a sale, the grantee or a representative files a statement declaring the value of the property (R.C. 319.202). The grantor pays the state conveyance fee, and also pays any real property transfer tax a county has levied under Chapter 322.

R.C. 319.54(G)(3) sets the conveyance fee at one dollar, or ten cents for each one hundred dollars or fraction of value, whichever is greater. R.C. 322.02 lets a county commission levy an added tax of up to thirty cents per hundred dollars. Ask the Sandusky County Auditor which combined rate it collects on the day you record, because this page does not quote a county rate.

Several kinds of transfers carry no conveyance fee. The statute lists these among others:

  • a transfer made only to give or release security for a debt
  • a deed that confirms or corrects a deed already recorded
  • a gift between spouses, or between a parent and child
  • a transfer made under a court order, unless it results from a sale
  • a transfer where no money or other valuable consideration changes hands and it is not a gift
  • a transfer among heirs or devisees of one decedent for no money

When a deed is exempt, the statement must give the reason for the exemption. The state's DTE 100(EX) form is the exemption version.

sections.h2: Can I record a Sandusky County deed electronically?
sections.html:
Yes. The recorder's office accepts electronic recording, and a submitter registers with one of the approved eRecording providers named on the county's vendor sheet: ePN, CSC eRecording, Simplifile and Hopdox. Title companies and attorneys usually already hold an account with one of them.

If no title company is involved, you can present the paper deed at the Fremont counter instead. Land records can be searched through the county's public search link on the recorder's page, which makes it easy to confirm your own legal description before you draft a deed.

sections.h2: What does the Census Bureau report about Sandusky County housing?
sections.html:
Sandusky County covers 408.25 square miles of land and had an estimated 58,655 residents on July 1, 2025, down 0.4 percent from the April 2020 estimates base. QuickFacts lists 26,530 housing units and 24,686 households for 2020 to 2024.

  • Owner-occupied housing unit rate: 73.4 percent
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $160,700
  • Median gross rent: $783
  • Median household income: $62,295
  • Mean travel time to work: 20.7 minutes

With about three in four homes lived in by their owners, most deeds here describe a house someone occupies. The Sandusky River runs northeast through the county to Sandusky Bay on Lake Erie, so ask your title company to check the flood zone for a parcel near the water.

sections.h2: How do property taxes tie into a Sandusky County sale?
sections.html:
The Sandusky County Treasurer states that real estate taxes are always due on the third Friday in February and the second Friday in July. Because of House Bill 186, the second-half 2025 bills, payable in 2026, were due August 7, 2026, and that date has passed.

Your closing agent will ask the treasurer for the amount owed on the parcel and will set aside what must be paid from your proceeds. If a half-year is unpaid, ask for a payoff figure before you sign the listing or sale contract. The treasurer's site also links to sheriff sale notices and to the county land bank, both useful if the house has come through a tax foreclosure or sits in a neighborhood the land bank works in.

faqs.q: Who records deeds in Sandusky County, Ohio?
faqs.a: The Sandusky County Recorder, at 100 N. Park Ave., Room 143, in Fremont. The office is open 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM Monday through Friday and can be reached at (419) 334-6226.

faqs.q: Does the deed go to the auditor or the recorder first?
faqs.a: The auditor comes first. Ohio law has the grantee file a statement of value with the county auditor, and the grantor pays the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax, before the deed is presented to the recorder for recording.

faqs.q: What is the recording fee for a deed in Ohio?
faqs.a: R.C. 317.32 prints a base fee of $17 plus a $17 housing trust fund fee for the first two pages, and $4 plus $4 for each added page. A county can add a preservation surcharge of up to $5, so ask the Sandusky County Recorder for the current posted total.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed in Sandusky County by e-recording?
faqs.a: Yes, through a provider the recorder has approved: ePN, CSC eRecording, Simplifile or Hopdox. Most homeowners reach it through a title company or attorney rather than registering on their own.

faqs.q: What happens if a deed is never recorded?
faqs.a: Under R.C. 5301.25, an unrecorded deed is treated as fraudulent against a later good-faith buyer who had no knowledge of it. The buyer can lose priority, so record the deed promptly after closing.
